records.sourceFile: Return to play and performance after primary ACL reconstruction in American football players - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Ross BJ, Savage-Elliott I, Brown SM, Mulcahey MK. Return to Play and Performance After Primary ACL Reconstruction in American Football Players: A Systematic Review. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2020;8(10):2325967120959654.
paper.abstract: This systematic review synthesized return-to-play and performance outcomes after primary ACL reconstruction in American football players.
paper.tldr: About two-thirds of included American football players returned after ACL reconstruction, with a mean return time of 11.6 months and generally worse postinjury performance than controls. Use this for expectation setting, not an individual timeline or clearance rule.
paper.methods: The authors searched five databases for English-language studies since 2000 reporting return, performance, or career length after primary ACL reconstruction in American football. Seventeen studies met inclusion criteria.
paper.findings: Return to play was 67.2% (1249/1859), and mean return time was 11.6 months (range 35.8-55.8 weeks). Across heterogeneous comparisons, most players had greater postinjury performance declines than controls over the same period.
paper.limitations: Studies varied in players, outcomes, controls, and definitions; many did not separate isolated reconstruction from concomitant procedures. Evidence was predominantly observational and professional-football focused.
paper.practicalImplications: Use sport- and position-specific expectations alongside individual clinical and performance progress. Plan a graded route from rehabilitation to football exposure rather than promising return from a pooled rate or calendar milestone.
paper.athleteDev: Explain that return and return to previous performance are different outcomes. Build confidence through transparent progression targets while acknowledging that role, prior performance, and recovery course affect the path.
paper.rtp: Combine symptoms, examination, strength, power, movement quality, psychological readiness, conditioning, position demands, and progressive practice exposure. The review does not support a single time point or test for clearance.

records.sourceFile: Effects of Far-Infrared Radiation-Lamp Therapy on Recovery From Simulated Soccer Match Running Activities in Elite Soccer Players.pdf

paper.citation: Hsieh CC, Nosaka K, Chou TY, Hsu ST, Chen TC. Effects of Far-Infrared Radiation-Lamp Therapy on Recovery From Simulated Soccer Match Running Activities in Elite Soccer Players. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2022;17(9):1432-1438.
paper.abstract: This randomized trial examined far-infrared lamp therapy during recovery from repeated simulated soccer-match running in elite female players.
paper.tldr: In 24 elite female soccer players completing six daily simulated matches, far-infrared lamp therapy produced smaller performance decrements and lower soreness and creatine kinase than sham. It is promising but remains a small, simulated-load study.
paper.methods: Twenty-four elite female soccer players were assigned to far-infrared or sham therapy while completing a daily 90-minute Loughborough Intermittent Shuttle Test for six days. Strength, soreness, creatine kinase, jump, sprint, and Yo-Yo outcomes were monitored through 120 hours after the final test.
paper.findings: Compared with sham, the far-infrared group had smaller peak decrements in knee-extensor torque, countermovement jump, and Yo-Yo performance, smaller soreness and creatine kinase responses, and earlier recovery toward baseline.
paper.limitations: The parallel study was small, used simulated running and an unusually demanding six-day protocol, and involved only young elite women. Longer-term, clinical, and competition-transfer effects are unknown.
paper.practicalImplications: If considering far-infrared therapy, trial it as one monitored recovery option alongside sleep, nutrition, hydration, load planning, and athlete preference. Verify meaningful response rather than assuming a device benefit.
paper.athleteDev: Keep recovery habits centered on the basics athletes can execute consistently. Explain that a favorable marker response in one study does not make a modality mandatory or a replacement for workload management.
paper.rtp: Do not use far-infrared treatment as a tissue-healing or readiness criterion. During return, prioritize symptoms, tissue capacity, progressive soccer loading, and the athlete's response to each exposure.

records.sourceFile: High Return to Competition Rate After On-Field Rehabilitation in Competitive Male Soccer Players After ACL Reconstruction - GPS Tracking in 100 Consecutive Cases.pdf

paper.citation: Picinini F, Della Villa F, Tallent J, et al. High Return to Competition Rate After On-Field Rehabilitation in Competitive Male Soccer Players After ACL Reconstruction: GPS Tracking in 100 Consecutive Cases. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2025;13(3):23259671251320093.
paper.abstract: This case series described field-based rehabilitation workloads and return outcomes for male competitive soccer players after ACL reconstruction.
paper.tldr: A five-stage field programme was followed by 84% return to competition among 97 players with follow-up. Final-stage loads approached team training but stayed below match demands, reinforcing the need to progress beyond controlled field work.
paper.methods: One hundred male 11-a-side soccer players completed a criteria-based indoor-to-field ACL rehabilitation process. GPS, heart-rate, and activity data across five field stages were analyzed, and return outcomes were obtained by follow-up questionnaire and mixed models.
paper.findings: At least nine-month follow-up was available for 97 players; 84% returned to competition, including 100% of professionals and 80% of amateurs, and 10% sustained ACL reinjury. Final-stage workload aligned with team-training demand for several metrics but was lower than match-play demand.
paper.limitations: There was no comparator pathway, outcomes relied partly on questionnaire follow-up, and professionals and amateurs differed in workload and context. One specialist male-soccer cohort cannot establish that the programme or GPS targets caused return outcomes.
paper.practicalImplications: Use field GPS to document staged exposure and plan the remaining gap to team training and match play. Interpret workload with skill, movement quality, symptoms, strength, confidence, and football context.
paper.athleteDev: Show players how controlled speed, high-intensity running, acceleration, and deceleration build toward team demands. Completing a stage demonstrates progress, not immunity from reinjury.
paper.rtp: Progress from field rehabilitation to full team training and representative match demands. GPS supports exposure accounting but cannot replace clinical criteria, psychological readiness, or observed football performance.

records.sourceFile: Practice Patterns and Return-to-SportsTiming of National Football League Head Team Physicians for ACL Reconstruction.pdf

paper.citation: Arner JW, Bradley JP. Practice Patterns and Return-to-Sports Timing of National Football League Head Team Physicians for ACL Reconstruction. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2024;12(10):23259671241274139.
paper.abstract: This cross-sectional survey described ACL reconstruction and return-to-sport practices reported by NFL head team orthopaedic surgeons.
paper.tldr: All 32 NFL head team physicians responded: mean return timing was nine months, none allowed return before seven months, and nearly all used functional testing. These are practice patterns, not outcome-validated clearance criteria.
paper.methods: All 32 NFL head team orthopaedic surgeons were surveyed about graft preferences, augmentation procedures, return timing, functional testing, and experience.
paper.findings: Thirty-one respondents used ipsilateral bone-patellar tendon-bone autograft for primary reconstruction. Mean return-to-sport timing was nine months, none allowed return before seven months, and all but one used functional testing in decisions.
paper.limitations: A physician survey does not measure athlete outcomes, actual care delivery, reinjury, or performance and cannot compare grafts or tests. It represents a highly resourced elite professional setting.
paper.practicalImplications: Use the findings to inform discussion of how NFL surgeons report approaching ACL care, while maintaining a locally accountable, individualized decision process.
paper.athleteDev: Distinguish a reported average practice timeline from a personal clearance date. Encourage athletes to focus on progressive capacity and decision criteria they can influence.
paper.rtp: Time and functional testing can contribute to a decision, but neither the survey's seven-month floor nor a test result alone establishes readiness for American football.

records.sourceFile: Return to sport after surgical   treatment of Lisfranc injuries in athletes - A retrospective case series.pdf

paper.citation: Vopat BG, Vopat ML, van Dijk PAD, et al. Return to Sport after Surgical Treatment of Lisfranc Injuries in Athletes: A Retrospective Case Series. Kansas Journal of Medicine. 2019;12(4):141-145.
paper.abstract: This retrospective case series reported return-to-sport outcomes after open reduction and internal fixation of ligamentous Lisfranc injuries in athletes.
paper.tldr: Eight of 10 followed athletes returned after surgical fixation at a mean 29.4 weeks and reported 87% of prior function, but occasional sport pain was common. The small uncontrolled series cannot set a universal Lisfranc timeline.
paper.methods: Athletes aged 18 to 40 who received single-surgeon open reduction and screw fixation for ligamentous Lisfranc injury were identified retrospectively. Follow-up questionnaires captured return, timing, function, pain, and complications.
paper.findings: Ten athletes had follow-up; eight returned to sport at a mean 29.4 weeks (range 22-52) and reported 87% of prior function. Six of nine reported occasional sport pain, and two complications were reported.
paper.limitations: This was a very small retrospective single-surgeon series with selected recreational or competitive athletes and no nonoperative or alternative-procedure comparator. Self-reported outcomes do not establish readiness or long-term joint health.
paper.practicalImplications: Use the series to counsel that return can occur after fixation but residual symptoms may persist. Progress foot function, strength, loading tolerance, and sport tasks against the individual surgical and clinical course.
paper.athleteDev: Frame return as rebuilding confidence and function despite a variable timeline. Encourage early reporting of pain or difficulty as loading and sport tasks advance.
paper.rtp: Use tissue healing, symptoms, foot and ankle capacity, running and cutting progression, sport demands, and clinician assessment. A mean return week is not a release criterion.

records.sourceFile: Cervical and Lumbar Disk Replacement in Athletes - Is It Safe to Return to Play - A systematic review of the scientific literature and lay press.pdf

paper.citation: Jo J, Davidar AD, Hersh AM, Theodore N, Zuckerman SL. Cervical and Lumbar Disk Replacement in Athletes: Is It Safe to Return to Play? A Systematic Review of the Scientific Literature and Lay Press. Neurosurgery. 2023.
paper.abstract: This systematic review summarized reported return to play after cervical or lumbar total disk replacement in athletes and supplemented sparse scientific reports with lay-press cases.
paper.tldr: Reported athletes generally returned after disk replacement, but evidence for contact sport rests on very few, selected cases. It cannot establish broad safety or a standard return pathway.
paper.methods: The authors used PRISMA-guided searches of five scientific databases for athlete total-disk-replacement reports and separately searched lay press; sports were classified by contact level.
paper.findings: Ten scientific studies described 53 cervical and 51 lumbar disk-replacement athletes. Reported professional and semiprofessional athletes generally returned without complication; across scientific literature and lay press, 14 professional contact-sport athletes were identified.
paper.limitations: Evidence was sparse and composed mainly of case reports and small retrospective cohorts, with selected athletes, variable procedures and follow-up, few contact-sport cases, and potential publication bias from successful reports.
paper.practicalImplications: Use specialist spine consultation and shared risk discussion when considering sport after disk replacement. Build decisions from procedure details, neurological status, imaging, sport contact exposure, and athlete goals.
paper.athleteDev: Communicate uncertainty honestly: a reported successful return in another athlete is not a prediction of safety or performance for an individual.
paper.rtp: Return after spine surgery requires injury- and procedure-specific specialist clearance, neurological and functional assessment, graduated sport exposure, and an explicit discussion of contact risk.

records.sourceFile: Groin pain in athletes and non-interventional rehabilitative treatment - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Ramazzina I, Bernazzoli B, Braghieri V, Costantino C. Groin Pain in Athletes and Non-Interventional Rehabilitative Treatment: A Systematic Review. Journal of Sports Medicine and Physical Fitness. 2019;59(6):1001-1010.
paper.abstract: This systematic review evaluated non-interventional rehabilitation approaches for athletes with groin pain.
paper.tldr: Low-certainty evidence favored active over passive treatment for clinical signs, and multimodal treatment was associated with faster return than active treatment alone. The review could not provide a best-practice algorithm.
paper.methods: Six electronic sources were searched from January 1997 through March 2017. Included studies were reviewed for participants, interventions, outcomes, retention, adverse effects, and methodological quality.
paper.findings: Randomized trials indicated active treatment outperformed passive treatment for clinical signs. Compared with active treatment, multimodal treatment allowed faster return to sport; the authors described integrating pain assessment, running progression, and sport-specific exercise.
paper.limitations: Evidence was poor and heterogeneous in diagnosis, intervention, dose, outcome, and quality, preventing practice guidelines or identification of one optimal algorithm.
paper.practicalImplications: First classify the athlete's groin presentation and rule out relevant pathology, then tailor progressive active loading, running, sport exposure, and selected adjuncts to response.
paper.athleteDev: Help athletes track symptoms and loading response while gradually restoring running and sport tasks. Avoid labeling all groin pain as the same problem or expecting one standard programme to fit every case.
paper.rtp: Return should reflect symptom behavior, capacity, running and change-of-direction tolerance, sport-specific demands, and diagnostic context—not completion of a generic multimodal programme.

records.sourceFile: Lower extremity return to sport testing - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Smiley T, Dallman J, Long R, et al. Lower Extremity Return to Sport Testing: A Systematic Review. The Knee. 2024;50:115-146.
paper.abstract: This systematic review mapped joint-specific and global lower-extremity testing used before return to sport after injury.
paper.tldr: Across 114 studies, return testing was overwhelmingly knee and ACL focused, with isokinetic dynamometry most common and no uniform clearance criterion. Hip and ankle evidence was notably limited.
paper.methods: PRISMA-guided searches of five databases through May 2024 identified 114 eligible studies from 19,189 records; ROBINS-I was used for risk-of-bias assessment.
paper.findings: Eighty-five percent of studies addressed knee pathology and 82% ACL reconstruction. Isokinetic dynamometry appeared in 73% of studies, whereas only 6.2% addressed hip pathology and two studies addressed ankle injury; no standardized return criterion was identified.
paper.limitations: Injury, sport, test, threshold, and outcome heterogeneity was substantial, and the literature was dominated by ACL/knee evidence. The review does not validate a universal battery's ability to reduce reinjury.
paper.practicalImplications: Select a joint- and sport-relevant battery that includes strength, functional performance, movement, symptoms, and patient-reported readiness, then interpret results in the athlete's exposure context.
paper.athleteDev: Explain why multiple measures may be needed and why a symmetric score or one successful test is progress rather than a universal pass-fail answer.
paper.rtp: Use testing to identify remaining deficits and guide progression to practice and competition. Clearance requires integrated clinical, performance, psychological, and sport-demand judgment.

records.sourceFile: Team Physician Consensus Statement - Return to Sport-Return to Play and the Team Physician - A Team Physician Consensus Statement - 2023 Update.pdf

paper.citation: Herring SA, Putukian M, Kibler WB, et al. Team Physician Consensus Statement: Return to Sport/Return to Play and the Team Physician: A Team Physician Consensus Statement-2023 Update. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2024.
paper.abstract: This consensus statement updates the team physician's role in return-to-sport decision-making across injuries, illnesses, sports, and athlete populations.
paper.tldr: Return is a context-dependent continuum from participation to sport to performance. The consensus favors an athlete-centered shared decision process led by the team physician and attentive to health, risk, goals, and coercion.
paper.methods: A multidisciplinary team-physician group produced an updated consensus statement addressing the return-to-sport process and decision responsibilities.
paper.findings: The statement characterizes return as ongoing and responsive to evolving information and risk. It recommends shared decision-making that incorporates diagnosis, individual risk, evidence-based options, athlete goals, sport context, and protection from coercion.
paper.limitations: This is consensus guidance, not an injury-specific comparative outcome study. It offers no validated universal thresholds, timelines, or probabilities, and implementation varies by setting.
paper.practicalImplications: Create a documented, athlete-centered process that names decision roles, considers health and sport risk, and revisits the plan as new information emerges.
paper.athleteDev: Invite athletes to express goals, questions, and concerns while clarifying that shared decision-making does not transfer medical responsibility or turn return into a simple vote.
paper.rtp: Use the continuum to stage participation, sport, and performance exposure. Pair it with injury-specific assessment and resist pressure to translate consensus principles into automatic clearance.

records.sourceFile: Topical glyceryl trinitrate for the treatment of tendinopathies- a systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Challoumas D, Kirwan PD, Borysov D, et al. Topical Glyceryl Trinitrate for the Treatment of Tendinopathies: A Systematic Review. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2019;53(4):251-262.
paper.abstract: This systematic review synthesized randomized trials of topical glyceryl trinitrate for tendinopathy.
paper.tldr: Ten randomized trials suggested some midterm benefits of topical glyceryl trinitrate versus placebo, but evidence varied by outcome and headaches were more common. It is an adjunct consideration, not a replacement for progressive loading.
paper.methods: MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, and CINAHL were searched through January 2018 for randomized trials comparing topical glyceryl trinitrate with placebo or other treatment. The authors assessed validity, external validity, precision, and evidence level.
paper.findings: Ten trials covered rotator cuff, wrist extensor, Achilles, and patellar tendinopathy. Short-term pain improvement had poor evidence; midterm satisfaction and asymptomatic daily activity had strong evidence, range and strength moderate evidence, and headaches were more frequent.
paper.limitations: Trials were few and heterogeneous in tendon, dose, comparator, cointervention, chronicity, quality, and outcome. The evidence was not return-to-sport-specific and does not define optimal dose, safety, or superiority to loading.
paper.practicalImplications: If a qualified clinician considers topical glyceryl trinitrate, use it as a monitored adjunct to diagnosis and progressive loading while screening contraindications, interactions, and headache tolerance.
paper.athleteDev: Set expectations that symptom change and tendon adaptation require time and progressive work. Athletes should report headaches or other adverse effects rather than altering medication use independently.
paper.rtp: Do not use a topical adjunct as evidence of tissue readiness. Advance sport exposure from tendon symptoms, capacity, function, load tolerance, and task-specific performance.

records.sourceFile: Meniscus tears in elite athletes - Treatment considerations, clinical outcomes, and return to play.pdf

paper.citation: Marigi EM, Davies MR, Marx RG, Rodeo SA, Williams RJ III. Meniscus Tears in Elite Athletes: Treatment Considerations, Clinical Outcomes, and Return to Play. Current Reviews in Musculoskeletal Medicine. 2024;17:313-320.
paper.abstract: This narrative review summarizes treatment considerations, clinical outcomes, and return-to-play issues for meniscus tears in elite athletes.
paper.tldr: Partial meniscectomy may allow faster return, while repair is preferred for anatomically repairable tears to preserve meniscus and protect long-term joint health. Treatment and timeline must be individualized.
paper.methods: The authors narratively reviewed contemporary literature on meniscus injury epidemiology, nonoperative and surgical treatment, and return-to-play outcomes in elite athletes.
paper.findings: The review reports a shift toward preservation because of concern for cartilage degeneration. Partial meniscectomy can provide quicker return, while repair has similar reported return rates and return to preinjury level in some literature; allograft transplantation is a salvage option with variable outcomes.
paper.limitations: This narrative review draws on heterogeneous, largely observational reports with different tears, procedures, sports, return definitions, and follow-up. It cannot identify a universally superior treatment or timeline.
paper.practicalImplications: Match treatment and rehabilitation to tear pattern, location, repairability, concomitant injury, knee stability, season demands, and the athlete's long-term joint goals.
paper.athleteDev: Help athletes understand the tradeoff between speed of return and meniscal preservation. Keep the discussion focused on their tear, role, goals, and long-term knee health rather than another athlete's timeline.
paper.rtp: Progress from symptoms and knee function to strength, movement, conditioning, and representative sport demands. A procedure label or early return rate does not establish individual readiness.
